name: Ivan Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Ivan. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say stays confidential. What do you do for work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker for the power company that runs the lines down from the hydro dams in the mountains. I'm on the maintenance side, high-voltage lines over passes and along the valley, about a year and a half in. Still very much learning.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the weather, always. On a good day we drive up the valley road to a tower, I help set up the gear, and the senior guys do the climbing while I learn the procedures for working near live lines, which is a whole world of rules. Our crew has started using a drone to look at insulators before we climb, and since I fly drones at the weekend for fun, I've become the drone guy. I love the mountains and the feeling of being trusted with something serious. What wears me out is the paperwork and the snow days when we sit in the depot doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, that's a shame, but it was always going to be slower than the hype. I'd probably post something like 'the robots aren't coming, back to the towers'. I'm not an AI fanboy, I just like tools that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's fine for me either way. The lines need maintaining, the dams aren't going anywhere. I'd just have fewer cool toys than I hoped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. Finish my ticket, keep being the drone guy, keep using AI to help with my study notes and to check the procedures. I'd keep putting money into my funds, about 500 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe slightly disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI right now, day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it to quiz me on the live-line procedures before my exams, and to turn my messy notes into a checklist. Sometimes I ask it about drone regulations. I always check the official manual, though, because one wrong answer up there and you're not coming home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your financial situation look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got about a year of costs in savings, and some money in a couple of broad share funds. My partner, Lena, is an accountant, and she's made me boringly sensible with money. The pay here is good because of the remote allowance.

S0.say: Ivan would say it was always going to be slower than the hype and post that crews are back to the towers. He describes himself as someone who likes tools that work, not an AI fan.
S0.think: Privately he's fine either way, since the hydro lines will always need maintaining. He'd just have fewer new tools than he hoped.
S0.do: Keeps working toward his ticket, flying the crew's drone and using AI for study notes and procedure checks. Continues investing about 500 a month in share funds.
S0.quote: I always check the official manual, though, because one wrong answer up there and you're not coming home.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is an early adopter who stays disciplined about safety and checks AI against the manual. His partner keeps his finances careful. His job security comes from the dams and the remote setting, not from technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for anyone willing to learn. The work gets safer if machines do the dangerous looking-around bits. I'd say that to the older guys too, gently, because some of them are nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's an opportunity. Drone inspections, AI spotting cracks in insulators from photos, robots doing the risky jobs near live lines. I'm already halfway into that, so I'd move toward running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my full commercial drone licence in the first couple of months, I've already looked at the course, it's about 1,200. I'd ask my supervisor to put me forward for any trial of inspection robots. And I'd probably start a small weekend side business doing drone surveys for farms and roofs, just to build experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Pretty excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would find it hardest on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, our oldest climber. He's 58, brilliant, and he still writes everything in a little notebook. I've tried to show him the drone footage and he just says he trusts his own eyes. I don't think he'd fight it, I think he'd just retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be going for a promotion-type role while still junior on the climbing. Any worry there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. I'm not a great climber yet, and I'd hate to be the guy who only knows the screen. I'd try to keep getting my climbing hours in, even if the drone stuff took more of my time.

S1.say: Ivan would say steady change is good news for anyone willing to learn, since machines can take over dangerous inspection work. He'd say so gently to nervous older colleagues.
S1.think: Privately he sees it as an opportunity: drone inspections, AI spotting insulator cracks and robots near live lines. He's already halfway into that and would move toward running it.
S1.do: Takes a commercial drone licence course costing about 1,200 within two months and asks to join any inspection robot trial. Starts a weekend drone survey side business for farms and roofs.
S1.quote: I've tried to show him the drone footage and he just says he trusts his own eyes.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan moves quickly and spends his own money to get ahead, while staying aware that his climbing is weak. His centre outlook shows as practical optimism rather than politics. His affection for his oldest colleague came through, along with a realistic guess about his choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be messy, and people need to keep their heads. I'd say governments should step in with some kind of support, because two years is not enough for people to adjust on their own. I'm not normally a 'government fix it' person, but that's too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd land on my feet for a while, because I know the drones and the tools. But it's the speed that bothers me. Lena's job is basically spreadsheets, and that goes first. And I'm junior on the lines, so if the robots work, they don't need me for long either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get onto whatever team brings the robots onto our lines in the first months, even if it meant moving to head office in the city. I'd put more money into the share funds, especially companies building the machines, because if the robots do the work, owning a little of them makes sense. And Lena and I would hold off on any big decisions, like buying a place, for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for me, really, but the whole thing feels like a car going too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put more into shares in a crisis. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But I've got a year of cash, and Lena would make me keep that untouched. The extra would come from what we'd saved for a flat. If the robots are doing the work, I'd rather own a piece of them than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably to take the early retirement if they offer it, and not to feel bad about it. He's done forty years up there. He's earned a quiet garden.

S2.say: Ivan would say it'll be messy and people must keep their heads, and that government support is needed because two years is too fast to adjust alone, despite his usual reluctance to call for state help.
S2.think: Privately he expects to land on his feet for a while through his drone and tech skills. The speed bothers him, along with his partner's spreadsheet-based job and his own junior status.
S2.do: Tries within months to join the team bringing robots onto the lines, even if it means moving to head office. Moves flat savings into shares in robot-building companies while keeping a year of cash, and delays buying a home.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like riding in a car that's going too fast.
S2.quote: If the robots are doing the work, I'd rather own a piece of them than nothing.
S2.fieldNote: Even with two years' warning, Ivan's instinct is to move toward the change and buy a stake in it. He bends his usual centre views to call for government support because of the speed. His unease is about pace and his partner, not his own competence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent amount of time if people start now. I'd tell the younger guys at the depot to learn the drones and the software, and the older ones to think about their pensions. Practical stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one might be the best for me. I get my ticket, three or four years of real experience, and I'm already the tech guy. By 2031 I'd want to be leading a robot maintenance team, not being replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the commercial drone licence and the side business. I'd look for a course in robotics or automation, maybe part-time at the technical college in the city. I'd keep investing steadily, and Lena and I would probably buy a small flat, because five years is enough time to plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a challenge I'm set up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, Lena's job worries you. Is that different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. With five years she can move into something like auditing the AI systems, she's already talked about it. With two, she wouldn't have time to turn around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that does bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The end, I suppose. Even if I'm leading the robot team, eventually the robots lead the robot team. But that's after 2031, and I'll deal with it then.

S3.say: Ivan would call five years a decent amount of time if people start now, telling young colleagues to learn drones and software and older ones to think about pensions.
S3.think: Privately he thinks this may be the best picture for him: qualified, experienced and already the tech person. By 2031 he wants to lead a robot maintenance team.
S3.do: Gets his commercial drone licence, grows the side business and enrols in a part-time robotics or automation course at the city technical college. Keeps investing and buys a small flat with his partner.
S3.feel: Calm, like facing a challenge he's ready for.
S3.quote: Even if I'm leading the robot team, eventually the robots lead the robot team.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives both Ivan and his partner time to change direction, which lifts his mood. He's aware that his plan only delays the end point and says so with humour. His advice to colleagues splits neatly by age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for being caught out with ten years' notice. Learn something, save something, plan something. I'd probably post a few videos of the drone work to get people interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really comfortable. Ten years to build skills, savings and maybe a business. The only question is what I want to be at 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd mostly focus on getting good at the actual line work, because there'd be time. I'd keep the side business going and keep investing. Around year three or four I'd start the automation course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty relaxed about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want to be at 37?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running my own small company that maintains robot crews for the power companies. Or maybe just a senior guy who knows the machines inside out. Ask me again in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still go to head office, like in the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd stay in the mountains. With ten years, I'd rather be good up here first. Head office would still be there in 2032.

S4.say: Ivan would say there's no excuse for being caught out with ten years' notice and urge people to learn, save and plan. He'd post drone videos to get others interested.
S4.think: Privately he'd feel very comfortable, with a decade to build skills, savings and perhaps a business. His only question is who he wants to be at 37.
S4.do: Focuses in the first year on getting good at hands-on line work while keeping his side business and investments going. Plans to start an automation course around year three or four.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd rather be good up here first. Head office would still be there in 2032.
S4.fieldNote: With a long runway, Ivan chooses craft first and technology later, the reverse of the fast picture. He stays in the mountains rather than moving to the city. He is open about not yet knowing what he wants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, mainly because of Lena and the speed of it. What would help is short-term income support for people while they switch, and the company training its own people on the robots instead of hiring outside.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but up near live lines, the first question should be whether the robot is safer than us. If it is, honestly, my mum would sleep better.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about jobs, but up near live lines, the first question should be whether the robot is safer than us.
portrait: Ivan Ibrahim is a 27-year-old junior on a high-voltage maintenance crew below the hydro dams, already the crew's drone pilot because he flies them for fun at weekends. He uses AI daily for study but always checks it against the manual, and his partner Lena, an accountant, keeps him sensible with money: a year saved plus share funds. He's practical, mid-road politically, and moves toward change early, planning a drone side business and a part-time automation course. He's calm in almost every picture and only uneasy when AGI arrives in two years, worried more about speed and his partner's job than about himself.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because of the speed and the risk to his partner's office job.
whatWouldHelp: Short-term income support while people switch, and the company training its own workers on the robots instead of hiring from outside.
